blocks.x: In over three years at Collider, senior author Jake has now penned over 3000 articles covering a wide range of TV and film for the resources, lists, utilities, news, and interview teams. Alongside interviewing stars such as Selin Hizli, Rose Ayling-Ellis, Harlan Coben, and Chelsea Peretti, Jake was lucky enough to visit the set of Aardman and Netflix's Wallace and Gromit: A Vengeance Most Fowl in 2024, getting the chance to chat with four-time Academy Award winner Nick Park and Merlin Crossingham. Jake has also worked for other publications, including Agents of Fandom. You can also hear Jake every week as the resident film and TV journalist on Track Radio.

We're just a couple of months away from the biggest date in the 2026 sci-fi calendar. On December 18, on the same date as Avengers: Doomsday, Dune: Part Three will cap off Denis Villeneuve's acclaimed trilogy adapting Frank Herbert's Dune novels. Four-time Oscar nominee Timothée Chalamet returns as Paul Atreides in the Brian K. Vaughan-penned movie, joined by a stacked cast including Zendaya as Chani, Javier Bardem as Stilgar, Rebecca Ferguson as Lady Jessica, Anya Taylor-Joy as Alia Atreides, Florence Pugh as Princess Irulan, Jason Momoa as Hayt, and many more.

But for Dune: Part Three to perform as some predicted and become the year's best sci-fi film, it faces tough competition from a novel adaptation that took the world by storm earlier this year. Of course, we're talking about arguably the defining film of 2026 so far, Project Hail Mary. The Phil Lord and Christopher Miller-directed masterpiece earned near-perfect responses from critics, including a 9/10 review from Collider's Ross Bonaime, who called it "the first great film of 2026."

But Project Hail Mary wasn't just an almighty success in the eyes of critics. In total, the adaptation of the 2021 novel by Andy Weir has earned $682 million worldwide, split between a domestic haul of $344 million and a further $338 million from overseas markets. This helped it become one of the year's earliest blockbuster triumphs, although the likes of Christopher Nolan's historical epic, The Odyssey, and Spider-Man: Brand New Day have since stolen that spotlight. But Project Hail Mary has moved seamlessly to streaming, becoming an unsurprising hit in homes around the world. At the time of writing, it has rejoined the Prime Video top ten in the U.S., ranking in ninth place.

Published Sep 21, 2026, 5:30 AM EDT

In over three years at Collider, senior author Jake has now penned over 3000 articles covering a wide range of TV and film for the resources, lists, utilities, news, and interview teams. Alongside interviewing stars such as Selin Hizli, Rose Ayling-Ellis, Harlan Coben, and Chelsea Peretti, Jake was lucky enough to visit the set of Aardman and Netflix's Wallace and Gromit: A Vengeance Most Fowl in 2024, getting the chance to chat with four-time Academy Award winner Nick Park and Merlin Crossingham. Jake has also worked for other publications, including Agents of Fandom. You can also hear Jake every week as the resident film and TV journalist on Track Radio.

Of course, we're talking about arguably the defining film of 2026 so far, Project Hail Mary. The Phil Lord and Christopher Miller-directed masterpiece earned near-perfect responses from critics, including a 9/10 review from Collider's Ross Bonaime, who called it "the first great film of 2026."

But Project Hail Mary wasn't just an almighty success in the eyes of critics. This helped it become one of the year's earliest blockbuster triumphs, although the likes of Christopher Nolan's historical epic, The Odyssey, and Spider-Man: Brand New Day have since stolen that spotlight. But Project Hail Mary has moved seamlessly to streaming, becoming an unsurprising hit in homes around the world. At the time of writing, it has rejoined the Prime Video top ten in the U.S., ranking in ninth place.

Your Crew Is…

Four ships, four completely different reasons to be up there at all.
Here is the one that has your seat, what flying with them would cost you, and what it would give
back.

Star Wars · Original Trilogy · Since 1977

Millennium Falcon

You belong on the fastest piece of junk in the galaxy, with a
crew that took the job for the payday and then quietly stopped caring about the payday.
Nothing on the Falcon has ever gone according to plan, and everybody aboard prefers it that
way.

You improvise better than you prepare, which is why you keep ending up in situations
that a careful person would have avoided.

The Falcon is the only ship on this list that is genuinely funny, and half of that comes
from it breaking at the worst possible moment.

You would pretend the whole thing is transactional right up until somebody you like is
in trouble, and then the pretending stops instantly.

This crew is the reason the rebellion had a chance at all, and not one of them would
ever admit to that out loud.

Star Wars Rebels · Disney XD · 2014 to 2018

The Ghost

You belong with the crew that turned a tiny cell of misfits into
an actual rebellion. The Ghost is a home before it is a ship, and everybody who boards it
arrived with something broken that the rest of them decided to look after.

Found family is the whole engine here, and Rebels earns it by making you watch these
people choose each other over and over again.

You are in it for the cause, but what actually keeps you going is the four people who
would notice immediately if you stopped showing up.

Hera is one of the best captains in the franchise, and the show is smart enough to make
her competence the quiet centre of everything.

This crew pays for its wins, which is exactly what makes the wins land the way they do.

Skeleton Crew · Disney+ · Since 2024

The Skeleton Crew

You belong with the four kids who found a buried ship, launched
it by accident and are now extremely lost in a galaxy that eats people like them. Nobody
here knows what they are doing, and that turns out to be the fun of it.

Your instinct is to open the door that says do not open, and you would do it again
tomorrow.

Skeleton Crew is the closest Star Wars has come to an eighties adventure movie, where
the stakes are real but the wonder never gets sanded off.

You make friends out of whoever is standing next to you when things go wrong, which is a
genuinely useful survival skill.

The pirates in this one are properly frightening, and that is precisely why the kids
being out of their depth works so well.

The Mandalorian · Disney+ · Since 2019

The Razor Crest

You belong in the quietest ship in the galaxy, with one small
passenger and a code you have never explained to anybody. You told yourself this was a job,
and then it stopped being a job somewhere around the second week.

You work alone by preference and by habit, which lasts exactly as long as it takes for
somebody small to need looking after.

The Mandalorian works because almost nothing gets said out loud, and the armour does the
acting that a face usually would.

Your loyalty is narrow and absolute, so there are very few people on your list and
nothing will move you off it.

The Mandalorian and Grogu took all of that to the big screen over Memorial Day 2026, the
first Star Wars film in seven years.
